Citizens Advice Guidance: Tenancy Deposits in Handover / Transfer Situations #### Does the Landlord / Agent Still Have to Protect Your Deposit? * **Statutory Obligation:** Yes. Under the Housing Act 2004, if you pay a tenancy deposit for an assured shorthold tenancy (AST) in England or Wales, your landlord or letting agent is legally required to protect it in a government-approved scheme within **30 calendar days** of receiving it. * **Third-Party / Handover Payments:** Protection is mandatory **even if someone else paid it for you** (e.g., parents, an employer, or an arrangement between incoming and outgoing tenants). * **Tenancy Takeover / Replacement Tenant Rules:** In a tenancy assignment or "change of sharer" handover, the landlord or letting agent cannot simply let an informal arrangement slide off the books. If a new tenancy agreement is created or an existing agreement is formally assigned to you, the deposit scheme records must be formally updated: * The scheme registration must reflect your name as the new tenant. * The landlord or agent must serve you with the official **"prescribed information"** (statutory details regarding the scheme, property, tenancy terms, and deposit dispute procedures) along with the deposit protection certificate, signed to confirm accuracy, within 30 days of the handover. * If the previous tenant's deposit was simply kept and you paid the outgoing tenant directly without scheme paperwork being transferred, the landlord remains legally accountable for ensuring the money is correctly held under your tenancy. #### How to Check Whether Your Deposit Is Protected There are three government-authorised tenancy deposit schemes in England and Wales. You can check each scheme's online tenancy database: 1. **Deposit Protection Service (DPS):** `depositprotection.com` 2. **MyDeposits:** `mydeposits.co.uk` 3. **Tenancy Deposit Scheme (TDS):** `tenancydepositscheme.com` **Search Details Required:** * The rental property postcode. * Your surname (and, if not found, the surname of the tenant you replaced or any joint tenants). * Tenancy start date (test both the date you moved in and the original tenancy start date). * Deposit amount. *Tip from Citizens Advice:* If the online automated checker returns no match, phone or email each scheme's customer service team directly. They can perform manual searches and provide written confirmation regarding whether a deposit has ever been registered for that address. #### What You Can Do If It Was Handled Incorrectly 1. **Financial Compensation (1 to 3 Times Deposit Value):** * Under Sections 213–214 of the Housing Act 2004, if the landlord or agent failed to protect your deposit within 30 days, failed to protect it at all, or failed to provide the signed prescribed information, a court can order them to repay the deposit plus pay compensation of **between 1 and 3 times the deposit amount**. * You can bring this claim in the County Court (using Form N208 under Part 8) at any time during the tenancy or up to **6 years** after the breach occurred. 2. **Eviction Protection:** * A landlord cannot evict you using a Section 21 "no fault" notice if they failed to protect the deposit on time or failed to issue the prescribed information, unless they return your full deposit to you first or court proceedings have concluded. 3. **Formal Letter Before Action:** * Before taking court action, Citizens Advice advises writing a formal letter to the landlord/agent stating: * They failed to comply with statutory deposit protection rules. * They could face a penalty of 1 to 3 times the deposit in court. * The specific remedy required (e.g., immediate return of your deposit or formal scheme certification). * A deadline of **21 days** to respond before court papers are filed. --- ### 2. Rent Ledger Setup: Structure & Columns for a Deposit Dispute #### What a Rent Ledger Is and Why Receipts Aren't Enough A rent ledger is a chronological, line-by-line accounting document tracking every debit (charge) and credit (payment), payment method, date, and outstanding balance between landlord and tenant. *Why Receipts Fall Short in Disputes:* * A bank receipt or transfer slip only proves a single isolated transaction; it does not prove the context or running account balance. * A ledger provides a timestamped, reconcilable audit trail proving whether rent was consistently paid on time, whether charges were assessed legitimately, and whether payments were allocated to deposit, fees, or rent. * In a County Court claim (Form N208) or deposit dispute, an ironclad ledger eliminates confusion over who paid what, when, and to whom. #### Tailored Rent Ledger Layout for a UK Tenancy & Deposit Handover Set up your spreadsheet (Excel or Google Sheets) with the following headers and tracking columns: **Account Header Block:** * Property Address & Room Number * Tenant Name(s) (including Outgoing Tenant Name if applicable) * Landlord & Letting Agent Names and Bank Account Details * Tenancy Start Date, Tenancy Takeover Date, and Rent Due Date * Monthly Rent Amount (£) and Agreed Tenancy Deposit Amount (£) **Recommended Columns:** 1. **Transaction Date:** Exact date payment left your bank or a charge was raised. 2. **Due Date:** Contractual due date per your tenancy agreement. 3. **Transaction Category / Description:** e.g., *Holding Deposit*, *Security Deposit*, *Handover / Assignee Fee*, *Rent Advance*, *Monthly Rent*. 4. **Billing Period Covered:** e.g., *Full Tenancy Deposit*, *01/10/2026 – 31/10/2026*. 5. **Amount Charged (£):** The amount legally due under the agreement. 6. **Amount Paid (£):** The actual amount transferred. 7. **Payment Method & Reference:** e.g., *Faster Payments, ref: "DEP-[Surname]"* or *Debit Card*. 8. **Payee Account / Recipient:** e.g., *Agent Client Account*, *Landlord Personal Account*, or *Direct to Outgoing Tenant [Name] (per agent written instruction)*. 9. **Running Rent Balance / Arrears (£):** Formula-driven (`Previous Balance + Charged - Paid`). Should show £0.00 to demonstrate no rent arrears exist. 10. **Scheme Protection Status & Cert ID:** Notes on compliance for that line item (e.g., *DPS Cert #XXXXXX*, *No certificate provided within 30-day window*, *TDS queried DD/MM/YYYY*). 11. **Evidence Reference / Appendix ID:** The file name or page number of corroborating evidence (e.g., *Bank Statement Oct 2026 Page 2*, *Agent Handover Confirmation Email*). --- ### 3. Practical Personal-Finance Strategies: Surviving Until Payday Drawing from financial guidance from **StepChange Debt Charity** and **Budget Wizard UK**, here are four realistic, non-destructive short-term ways to maintain cash flow without making your situation worse: 1. **Daily Per-Diem Envelope & "Consequence-First" Priority Triage:** * Count the exact number of days remaining until your next paycheck. Take your accessible cash (after mandatory rent/utilities) and divide it by the days left to establish a strict daily spending cap. * Rank all upcoming obligations by legal consequence: prioritize rent, council tax, and essential energy over unsecured debts (credit cards, loans). * Proactively contact non-priority service providers before a payment bounces to request a temporary payment deferral or moved billing date. Most utility and phone providers have formal breathing space/hardship arrangements. 2. **"Eat from the Pantry" Challenge & Redeeming Dormant Loyalty Points/Cashback:** * Conduct a full inventory of your freezer and cupboards and build a meal plan around existing dry goods and tins to reduce grocery outlays to zero or near-zero for 1–2 weeks. * Cash out accumulated balances from cashback platforms (e.g., TopCashback, Quidco) into your bank account. * Convert supermarket reward points (Tesco Clubcard vouchers, Sainsbury's Nectar points, Boots Advantage points) directly at the till to cover essential groceries or hygiene items. 3. **Fast Local Asset Liquidation (Zero Debt):** * Sell unused electronics, clothes, or small household items via immediate local collection channels (Facebook Marketplace, Gumtree, or instant buy-back stores like CeX) to generate quick, debt-free cash. 4. **Avoid High-Cost Credit & Check Non-Repayable Local Welfare:** * Avoid payday loans, logbook loans, or high-interest overdrafts, which turn temporary timing mismatches into recurring debt spirals. * If facing an acute food or heating shortfall, contact your local council for access to the **Household Support Fund**, local discretionary welfare assistance, or check local community pantries/food banks for temporary emergency relief. --- ### 4. By now, you might be looking at all of the details you need to include in your rent ledger and wonder whether doing so is worth the hassle. After all, in the age of digital banking, we have receipts for rent payments to keep everything straight… right?
 
As convenient as it may seem to rely solely on receipts, a single receipt can only confirm a single payment. Keeping an up-to-date rent ledger, on the other hand, will reveal patterns over time and indicate whether a tenant is in good standing or may soon face payment problems.
 
Without a ledger, you might never know that a tenant has been consistently paying rent a few days late. Further, you’ll have a harder time charging and enforcing late rent fees, and you might even lose track of which tenants have and haven’t paid their full rent.
 
A current rent ledger includes three important details that receipts don’t:
 
Missed payments show up right away
Chronic lateness and other payment patterns are easy to see
Late fee history shows whether a landlord assessed fees consistently
For landlords tracking rental payments across multiple properties, the ledger helps support process-driven rental property accounting and makes it a breeze to fill out a Schedule E come tax time. And since the IRS requires landlords to keep records of rental income and expenses, a reconciled ledger does more for compliance than a stack of receipts ever could.
Common Mistakes With Rent Ledgers
As useful as rent ledgers can be, they’re only worthwhile if you update them frequently and properly. Here are a few common mistakes that landlords should watch out for:
 
Tracking only payments and skipping charges: Without a record of the amount charged, there’s no way to prove how much the tenant actually owes.
Inconsistently documenting late fees: Landlords who fail to document all late-fee charges will struggle to maintain the transparency and reasonableness required by law.
Logging a partial payment as a full payment: Incorrectly logging partial payments as full payments creates an accounting imbalance, making it more difficult to obtain the full amount owed.
Mixing multiple properties on one sheet: Keeping all properties and tenants on one ledger sheet is a mix-up waiting to happen, since it’s easy to confuse payment details between renters and units.
Updating the ledger once a month: Ledgers should be updated whenever a charge or payment is made to ensure up-to-date recordkeeping.
Overwriting or deleting an incorrect entry: Deleting and overwriting can be confusing, so instead create a new entry that reverses the previous incorrect data.
Not holding on to supporting documents: Landlords should always retain documents (including those receipts we mentioned) that corroborate the information within the rent ledger.
With a little forethought, you can easily prevent each of these seven mistakes from happening. If you’re not careful, though, you could end up facing conflicts with your tenants and potential legal trouble.

Landlords generally have two choices when creating a rent ledger: dedicated rental accounting software or a spreadsheet. Both of these options cover the necessary basics, but you’ll want to keep a few details in mind as you decide which one would be best for your rental business:

What To Do If You Run Out of Money Before Payday

Running out before payday is stressful, but the next move matters. This guide helps you protect essentials and avoid decisions that make next month harder.

6 min read
By Budget Wizard
1 Jun 2026
Beginner

Money Emergencies

Running out before payday is stressful, but the next move matters. This guide helps you protect essentials and avoid decisions that make next month harder.

Running out before payday is a cash-flow problem first. The key question is whether it is a one-off timing issue or evidence that regular commitments exceed regular income.

A practical way to work through it
Count exactly how many days remain until income arrives.
Ring-fence food, essential travel, medication and priority bills due before payday.
Check pending card payments and automatic debits.
Contact providers before a payment fails if you cannot cover it.
After payday, work out what caused the gap so you do not repeat the same month.
Example

If seven days remain and you have £70 after priority bills, that is a £10-a-day envelope for food and essential variable costs. The number is not comfortable, but it is clearer than spending normally for three days and then having nothing.

Your main options and trade-offs
Use existing cash or savings for a genuine one-off emergency.
Ask a provider to move a payment date if it offers that flexibility.
Reduce or pause non-essential spending.
Seek support rather than repeatedly using high-cost credit to bridge every month.
Use a consequence-first hierarchy

In a crisis, people often pay whichever company is making the most noise. A safer framework is to rank each payment by the consequence of not paying it. Losing housing, essential energy, a vehicle needed for work, or facing court or enforcement action can be more serious than damage to an unsecured-credit account. That is why 'priority debt' is about consequences rather than interest rate.

Create a one-page list with five columns: amount due, date due, whether it is a priority commitment, consequence of missing it, and who you need to contact. This turns a frightening pile of messages into a queue of decisions.

Know whether the problem is temporary or structural

A one-off £400 gap caused by an annual bill needs a different solution from a budget that is £400 short every month. For a temporary gap, rearranging payment dates, using an existing emergency fund or agreeing short-term arrangements may be enough. For a structural gap, repeated short-term borrowing usually delays the problem and adds cost. You need a sustainable change to spending, income, commitments or debt arrangements.

Stress-test the next 30 days
What cash is definitely available?
What income is definitely arriving, and on what date?
Which costs cannot safely be delayed?
Which payments can be negotiated?

Citizens Advice Guidance: Tenancy Deposits in Handover / Transfer Situations #### Does the Landlord / Agent Still Have to Protect Your Deposit? * **Statutory Obligation:** Yes. Under the Housing Act 2004, if you pay a tenancy deposit for an assured shorthold tenancy (AST) in England or Wales, your landlord or letting agent is legally required to protect it in a government-approved scheme within **30 calendar days** of receiving it. * **Third-Party / Handover Payments:** Protection is mandatory **even if someone else paid it for you** (e.g., parents, an employer, or an arrangement between incoming and outgoing tenants). * **Tenancy Takeover / Replacement Tenant Rules:** In a tenancy assignment or "change of sharer" handover, the landlord or letting agent cannot simply let an informal arrangement slide off the books. If a new tenancy agreement is created or an existing agreement is formally assigned to you, the deposit scheme records must be formally updated: * The scheme registration must reflect your name as the new tenant. * The landlord or agent must serve you with the official **"prescribed information"** (statutory details regarding the scheme, property, tenancy terms, and deposit dispute procedures) along with the deposit protection certificate, signed to confirm accuracy, within 30 days of the handover. * If the previous tenant's deposit was simply kept and you paid the outgoing tenant directly without scheme paperwork being transferred, the landlord remains legally accountable for ensuring the money is correctly held under your tenancy. #### How to Check Whether Your Deposit Is Protected There are three government-authorised tenancy deposit schemes in England and Wales. You can check each scheme's online tenancy database: 1. **Deposit Protection Service (DPS):** `depositprotection.com` 2. **MyDeposits:** `mydeposits.co.uk` 3. **Tenancy Deposit Scheme (TDS):** `tenancydepositscheme.com` **Search Details Required:** * The rental property postcode. * Your surname (and, if not found, the surname of the tenant you replaced or any joint tenants). * Tenancy start date (test both the date you moved in and the original tenancy start date). * Deposit amount. *Tip from Citizens Advice:* If the online automated checker returns no match, phone or email each scheme's customer service team directly. They can perform manual searches and provide written confirmation regarding whether a deposit has ever been registered for that address. #### What You Can Do If It Was Handled Incorrectly 1. **Financial Compensation (1 to 3 Times Deposit Value):** * Under Sections 213–214 of the Housing Act 2004, if the landlord or agent failed to protect your deposit within 30 days, failed to protect it at all, or failed to provide the signed prescribed information, a court can order them to repay the deposit plus pay compensation of **between 1 and 3 times the deposit amount**. * You can bring this claim in the County Court (using Form N208 under Part 8) at any time during the tenancy or up to **6 years** after the breach occurred. 2. **Eviction Protection:** * A landlord cannot evict you using a Section 21 "no fault" notice if they failed to protect the deposit on time or failed to issue the prescribed information, unless they return your full deposit to you first or court proceedings have concluded. 3. **Formal Letter Before Action:** * Before taking court action, Citizens Advice advises writing a formal letter to the landlord/agent stating: * They failed to comply with statutory deposit protection rules. * They could face a penalty of 1 to 3 times the deposit in court. * The specific remedy required (e.g., immediate return of your deposit or formal scheme certification). * A deadline of **21 days** to respond before court papers are filed. --- ### 2. Rent Ledger Setup: Structure & Columns for a Deposit Dispute #### What a Rent Ledger Is and Why Receipts Aren't Enough A rent ledger is a chronological, line-by-line accounting document tracking every debit (charge) and credit (payment), payment method, date, and outstanding balance between landlord and tenant. *Why Receipts Fall Short in Disputes:* * A bank receipt or transfer slip only proves a single isolated transaction; it does not prove the context or running account balance. * A ledger provides a timestamped, reconcilable audit trail proving whether rent was consistently paid on time, whether charges were assessed legitimately, and whether payments were allocated to deposit, fees, or rent. * In a County Court claim (Form N208) or deposit dispute, an ironclad ledger eliminates confusion over who paid what, when, and to whom. #### Tailored Rent Ledger Layout for a UK Tenancy & Deposit Handover Set up your spreadsheet (Excel or Google Sheets) with the following headers and tracking columns: **Account Header Block:** * Property Address & Room Number * Tenant Name(s) (including Outgoing Tenant Name if applicable) * Landlord & Letting Agent Names and Bank Account Details * Tenancy Start Date, Tenancy Takeover Date, and Rent Due Date * Monthly Rent Amount (£) and Agreed Tenancy Deposit Amount (£) **Recommended Columns:** 1. **Transaction Date:** Exact date payment left your bank or a charge was raised. 2. **Due Date:** Contractual due date per your tenancy agreement. 3. **Transaction Category / Description:** e.g., *Holding Deposit*, *Security Deposit*, *Handover / Assignee Fee*, *Rent Advance*, *Monthly Rent*. 4. **Billing Period Covered:** e.g., *Full Tenancy Deposit*, *01/10/2026 – 31/10/2026*. 5. **Amount Charged (£):** The amount legally due under the agreement. 6. **Amount Paid (£):** The actual amount transferred. 7. **Payment Method & Reference:** e.g., *Faster Payments, ref: "DEP-[Surname]"* or *Debit Card*. 8. **Payee Account / Recipient:** e.g., *Agent Client Account*, *Landlord Personal Account*, or *Direct to Outgoing Tenant [Name] (per agent written instruction)*. 9. **Running Rent Balance / Arrears (£):** Formula-driven (`Previous Balance + Charged - Paid`). Should show £0.00 to demonstrate no rent arrears exist. 10. **Scheme Protection Status & Cert ID:** Notes on compliance for that line item (e.g., *DPS Cert #XXXXXX*, *No certificate provided within 30-day window*, *TDS queried DD/MM/YYYY*). 11. **Evidence Reference / Appendix ID:** The file name or page number of corroborating evidence (e.g., *Bank Statement Oct 2026 Page 2*, *Agent Handover Confirmation Email*). --- ### 3.
